families.s: HSE human-performance controls for lighting, thermal comfort, space, noise and vibration
families.t: task lighting, colour, contrast, glare, temperature, workspace, communication noise, vibration and worker control
f: The work environment can affect health, task performance and attitudes.
Lighting levels should suit the detail and visual demands of the task.
Colour, contrast, glare and sudden changes in light level can affect safe performance.
Temperature extremes can create physiological stress, while lack of thermal control can affect satisfaction and stress.
Workrooms need enough free space for safe movement, access and storage.
Noise can interfere with safety-critical communication and contribute to stress.
Whole-body vibration can contribute to back pain and fatigue and may impair visual performance.
Local control of lighting and attention to actual equipment shadows can improve working conditions.
families.g: Task lighting, colour, contrast, glare, temperature, workspace, communication noise, vibration and worker control guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.t: leadership, management style, worker involvement, communication, competence, procedures, learning, measurement and feedback
f: Organisational culture can be understood as the way things are done in the workplace.
Culture influences human behaviour and performance.
Poor safety culture has contributed to major incidents and personal injuries.
Culture can influence safety outcomes as strongly as the formal safety-management system.
Management commitment and style are major influences on safety culture.
Worker involvement, competence, communication, procedure compliance and organisational learning are key influences.
Safety-climate measurement provides a snapshot and should be proportionate to the hazards.
Measurement should lead to action, feedback to workers and repeated checks of progress.
families.g: Leadership, management style, worker involvement, communication, competence, procedures, learning, measurement and feedback guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.t: safe behaviours, unsafe behaviours, observation, feedback, reinforcement, participation, management visibility and leading indicators
f: Behavioural-safety and behaviour-modification programmes are widely used.
Programmes commonly define safe and unsafe behaviours.
They normally include observation of behaviour in the workplace.
Observation may be conducted by managers, peers or both.
Programmes provide feedback and reinforce safer behaviour.
Behavioural approaches can increase management visibility.
They can promote workforce participation and constructive safety discussion.
Behavioural observations may provide leading indicators but should not replace controls for wider organisational and engineering causes.

families.s: HSE application and limitations of behaviour-modification approaches
families.t: participation, observations, targets, feedback, leadership, engagement, dangerous conditions and system context
f: Behavioural approaches are often adopted because unsafe behaviour is reported as a factor in accidents.
They can provide a vehicle for management and workforce participation.
Observed behaviour can influence attitudes, perceptions and organisational culture.
Programme features include agreed definitions of safe and unsafe behaviour.
Observation may use managers, peers, targets or no targets.
Feedback can range from immediate discussion to aggregated performance information.
Potential benefits include engagement, leadership learning and identification of dangerous situations.
Behavioural programmes should operate within a mature safety-management system and not focus blame solely on individuals.
families.g: Participation, observations, targets, feedback, leadership, engagement, dangerous conditions and system context guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE active organisational learning and corporate memory
families.t: incidents, near misses, external lessons, recommendations, active learning, weak signals, chronic unease and corporate memory
f: A learning organisation values lessons from its own experience and looks outside itself for learning.
Near misses, incidents and accidents should be investigated by trained people.
Lessons should be communicated widely.
Investigation recommendations should be implemented promptly.
Active learning embeds lessons into culture and practice rather than only identifying them.
Corporate memory should survive staff losses, organisational changes and contractorisation.
Learning organisations maintain chronic unease instead of becoming complacent.
They seek weak signals and information even where operations appear to be running smoothly.
